nameStory: The "trunk" in Trunk Pawwort refers to this liverwort's relatively thick, sturdy main stem that resembles a tiny tree trunk when viewed up close. The "pawwort" part comes from the old English tradition of calling liverworts "worts" (meaning plant), and this species' leaf-like structures can look like tiny paws reaching out from the stem.
description: Trunk Pawwort is a small leafy liverwort that forms delicate, branching mats on moist surfaces. This tiny non-flowering plant grows as flattened shoots with two rows of overlapping leaf-like structures along a central stem. The entire plant rarely exceeds an inch in length, creating intricate green carpets that require close inspection to fully appreciate. Like all liverworts, it reproduces by spores rather than seeds and lacks true roots.

idTips.label: Leaf arrangement
idTips.description: Two distinct rows of overlapping, scale-like leaves along the stem create a flattened, almost braided appearance when viewed from above

idTips.label: Stem texture
idTips.description: The main stem feels firm and slightly rigid compared to other liverworts, with a pale green to whitish color that stands out against the darker leaves

idTips.label: Leaf shape
idTips.description: Individual leaves are small, rounded to oval, and often slightly cupped, giving them a spoon-like feel when gently touched with a fingertip

idTips.label: Branching pattern
idTips.description: Branches fork in a Y-shaped pattern, creating irregular but symmetrical spreading mats that feel spongy underfoot

idTips.label: Overall texture
idTips.description: The entire plant has a soft, velvety texture when stroked gently, much smoother than surrounding mosses

habitat: Look for Trunk Pawwort on moist, shaded rocks and fallen logs in cool, humid forests throughout New England's mountains and hills. It particularly favors acidic substrates like decaying coniferous wood and granite surfaces near streams or seeps. This liverwort thrives in the consistent moisture and filtered light found under dense canopies of spruce, fir, and hemlock forests.

seasonality.spring: Fresh green growth appears as snow melts, with the plant looking its most vibrant and full. This is the best time to spot reproductive structures if present.
seasonality.summer: Continues growing actively in shaded, moist locations while remaining green and lush. May appear slightly smaller in drier periods.
seasonality.fall: Remains visible and identifiable, often with a slightly darker green coloration. Prepares for winter dormancy as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Persists under snow cover in a dormant state, sometimes visible during warm spells as dark green patches on exposed surfaces.

funFact: Despite being only 7 observations recorded in all of New England, Trunk Pawwort can survive being completely dried out for months and spring back to life within hours of getting wet again - a superpower that allows it to colonize seemingly impossible rocky crevices where no other plants can survive!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small mosses, but liverworts like Trunk Pawwort have distinctly flattened, two-ranked leaves while mosses have leaves arranged all around the stem. Memory trick: liverworts lie flat, mosses stand up all around.
contextualKnowledge: Liverworts are among Earth's oldest land plants, and finding species like Trunk Pawwort connects you to plant life that has remained virtually unchanged for over 400 million years. The extreme rarity of recorded observations doesn't necessarily mean it's endangered - liverworts are simply overlooked by most botanists due to their tiny size.
compareHints: Since Trunk Pawwort is the only Neoorthocaulis species in our region, compare it to other small leafy liverworts in the Anastrophyllaceae family by looking for its distinctively thick, pale stem and the precise two-ranked leaf arrangement. Most related liverworts have thinner, more delicate stems and less organized leaf patterns.
